cites.loc: "given command of India's only parachute brigade"
para 4

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: An infantry officer for the parachute brigade
claims.text: He came to 50 (Independent) Parachute Brigade in September 1961 from the 3rd Gorkha Rifles, an infantry officer rather than a paratrooper.

cites.loc: p. 65: 2 Sikh LI reached Panjim first; 1 Para, in maroon berets, reached the seat of government (Governor's house) first
"the first to reach the capital of Goa, Panjim on 19 December 1961"

claims.established: Units under Brigadier Sagat Singh's command were the first into Panjim (2 Sikh LI) and the first to the seat of government (1 Para) on 19 December 1961 (A Talent for War, p. 65).
claims.heading: Into Panjim and the seat of government

prev.heading: First into Panjim
prev.text: The brigade was the first to reach Panjim, on 19 December 1961.

claims.text: On 19 December 1961 his brigade was first on both counts: 2 Sikh Light Infantry, under his command, was the first unit to reach Panjim, and paratroopers of 1 Para, in maroon berets, were the first to reach the seat of government, the Governor's house.
claims.unresolved: Settled. Per the biography, 2 Sikh LI, under his command, entered Panjim first and 1 Para reached the Governor's house first; the SSRF founder confirms both units were under his command. Still to record: the time of each arrival.

cites.loc: p. 66: Salazar put a bounty of $10,000 on Sagat Singh's head for his role in Goa's liberation
the article's title

claims.established: His biography records a $10,000 bounty on his head, put by Salazar's Portugal (A Talent for War, p. 66).
claims.heading: A price on his head

prev.text: Portugal put a reward on his capture.

claims.text: Salazar's government in Portugal put a bounty of $10,000 on his head for his part in the liberation of Goa.
claims.unresolved: Now attributed to the standard biography (p. 66), which gives the amount and names Salazar. Popular accounts likely draw on the same source, so they do not count as independent. A Portuguese record of the bounty (a government notice, a newspaper of December 1961 or January 1962, or archive file) would make it documented.

cites.loc: the Indian Army marked his birth centenary on 14 July 2019
born in Kusumdesar (Moda), Churu district, on July 14, 1919
"born … in the village of Kusumdesar in Churu region of Bikaner State on 14 July 1919"

claims.established: Born on 14 July 1919 in Kusumdesar, Bikaner State.
claims.heading: Born in Kusumdesar
claims.text: Born on 14 July 1919 in Kusumdesar, in present-day Churu district of Rajasthan, then part of Bikaner State.

cites.loc: p. 19: enrolled as a Naik in the Bikaner State Forces' Ganga Risala by Lt Col Balu Singh Shekhawat on Maj Khem Singh's recommendation, after his intermediate exams in 1938
"enrolled as a Naik in the Bikaner Ganga Risala"
"In 1941, the unit landed at Basra"
"he received a commission as a Second Lieutenant from the King"
his son's account of his start as a Naik in 1938
para 4 says "Jaipur State Forces"; SSRF treats this as an error (see note)

claims.established: He served in the Bikaner State Forces, enrolling as a Naik in the Ganga Risala in 1938 (A Talent for War, p. 19), and was commissioned during the Second World War.
claims.familyNote: Confirmed with the family by the SSRF founder, 15 November 2026.
claims.heading: Bikaner State Forces

prev.established: He began in the ranks of a princely state's forces in 1938 and was commissioned during the Second World War.
prev.text: Enrolled as a Naik in the Bikaner Ganga Risala in 1938, after his intermediate examination. He moved with the Sadul Light Infantry, landed at Basra in 1941, and was commissioned during the Second World War.

claims.text: Enrolled as a Naik in the Bikaner Ganga Risala in 1938, immediately after his intermediate examination. The commanding officer, Lt Col Balu Singh Shekhawat, enrolled him on the recommendation of the second-in-command, Maj Khem Singh. He moved with the Sadul Light Infantry, landed at Basra in 1941, and was commissioned during the Second World War.
claims.unresolved: Settled: Bikaner State Forces, per A Talent for War p. 19, confirmed with the family. The 2001 PIB release's "Jaipur State Forces" is an error. Still to record: the exact date and rank of his commission.

cites.loc: p. 30: transferred to 3 Gorkha Rifles in February 1949; posted as GSO2
"In 1949, Singh was transferred to the Indian Army"
"In February 1955 … commanding officer of the second battalion 3rd Gorkha Rifles (2/3 GR) at Ferozepur"
para 4: joined "on amalgamation"

claims.established: He joined the 3rd Gorkha Rifles in February 1949 (A Talent for War, p. 30) and spent his regimental career with it.
claims.heading: Into the Indian Army and the 3rd Gorkha Rifles

prev.text: Transferred to the Indian Army and the 3rd Gorkha Rifles when the state forces were absorbed. He commanded the regiment's 2nd Battalion from February 1955, later its 3rd Battalion, and was Colonel of the Regiment from 1969 to 1976.

claims.text: Transferred to the 3rd Gorkha Rifles of the Indian Army in February 1949, when the Bikaner State Forces were absorbed, and posted as a General Staff Officer Grade 2 (GSO2). He commanded the regiment's 2nd Battalion from February 1955, later its 3rd Battalion, and was Colonel of the Regiment from 1969 to 1976.
claims.unresolved: Settled: February 1949, per A Talent for War p. 30, consistent with Wikipedia's 1949. Still to record: the formation or headquarters where he served as GSO2.

cites.loc: "In September 1961, Singh was promoted to the rank of brigadier"
"the first to reach the capital of Goa, Panjim on 19 December 1961"
para 5

claims.established: He commanded 50 Parachute Brigade in the liberation of Goa.
claims.heading: Liberation of Goa
claims.text: Promoted brigadier in September 1961 and given 50 (Independent) Parachute Brigade, India's only parachute brigade, which he led in Operation Vijay. The brigade reached Panjim (Panaji) on 19 December 1961.
claims.unresolved: Settled. Panjim on 19 December 1961: 2 Sikh LI into the town and 1 Para to the Governor's house, both under his command (A Talent for War, p. 65). The Portuguese bounty is recorded in the biography (p. 66).

cites.loc: "in July 1965, Singh was promoted to the rank of major general"
"Major General Sagat Singh, GOC 17 Mountain Division, refused to vacate Nathu La"
"the Nathu La and Cho La clashes took place, where 17 Mountain Division achieved"
1967 hierarchy: Manekshaw, Aurora, Sagat Singh

claims.established: He commanded 17 Mountain Division during the 1967 clashes at Nathu La and Cho La.
claims.heading: Nathu La and Cho La
claims.text: Promoted major general in July 1965 and given 17 Mountain Division in Sikkim. He refused to vacate Nathu La, and in 1967 the division held Nathu La and Cho La in clashes with Chinese troops.
claims.unresolved: Settled. The 1965 refusal to vacate Nathu La is recorded in A Talent for War (p. 74) and the UNI report. To record: whether his promotion to major general was in 1964 or 1965.

cites.loc: "In December 1967, Singh was appointed GOC 101 Communication Zone in Shillong"
para 5

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: Mizo Hills
claims.text: Appointed GOC 101 Communication Zone at Shillong in December 1967. The formation conducted operations against the insurgency in the Mizo Hills.

cites.loc: "on 26 January 1970, Singh was awarded the Param Vishisht Seva Medal"
"took over the command of IV Corps in December 1970"
para 5
sent to Tezpur, Assam

claims.established: He held the PVSM and took command of IV Corps in December 1970.
claims.heading: PVSM and IV Corps
claims.text: Awarded the Param Vishisht Seva Medal on 26 January 1970. In December 1970 he took command of IV Corps at Tezpur as a lieutenant general.
claims.unresolved: To add: the Gazette of India notification for the PVSM of 26 January 1970.

cites.loc: "the corps made the famous advance to Dhaka over the River Meghna"
"He witnessed in Dhaka the signing of the surrender instrument by General Niazi"
para 5

claims.established: He commanded IV Corps in the 1971 war, was present at the surrender and received the Padma Bhushan.
claims.heading: Across the Meghna to Dhaka
claims.text: His corps crossed the Meghna and advanced on Dhaka. He witnessed General Niazi sign the instrument of surrender on 16 December 1971, and received the Padma Bhushan in 1972 for the campaign.

cites.loc: p. 240: retired in November 1974
gives November 1974
para 4: Colonel of the Regiment, 1969 to 1976
"retired from the army on 30th November 1976" (incorrect year)

claims.established: He retired in November 1974 (A Talent for War, p. 240).
claims.heading: Retirement

prev.text: Retired from the Army on 30 November 1976, the year his term as Colonel of the 3rd Gorkha Rifles ended.

claims.text: Retired from the Army in November 1974. He remained Colonel of the 3rd Gorkha Rifles, an honorary regimental appointment, until 1976.
claims.unresolved: Settled on November 1974: the biography (p. 240) and Salute magazine agree. The 30 November 1976 date in an older encyclopaedia text confuses retirement with the end of his term as Colonel of the Regiment in 1976. To record: the exact day.

cites.loc: paras 1 and 6
"died at the Army Hospital Research and Referral, New Delhi on 26 September 2001"

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: Died in New Delhi
claims.text: Died on 26 September 2001 at the Army Hospital (Research and Referral), New Delhi.

cites.loc: "took over the command of IV Corps in December 1970"
para 5
sent to Tezpur, Assam

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: Command of IV Corps
claims.text: He took command of IV Corps at Tezpur as a lieutenant general in December 1970.

cites.loc: "made the decision to airlift the Indian troops"
"the corps made the famous advance to Dhaka over the River Meghna"

claims.established: IV Corps crossed the Meghna on its advance to Dhaka.
claims.heading: The airlift across the Meghna
claims.text: When the bridge on his line of advance was out of use, he and Maj Gen B F Gonsalves decided to airlift troops across the Meghna rather than wait for repairs.
claims.unresolved: To add: a second published account of the decision to airlift and its timing.

cites.loc: "conceptualised the Indian Army's first heliborne operation in the Battle of Sylhet"
a helicopter pilot's first-hand account of the Sylhet landings

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: The first heliborne operation
claims.text: He conceived the Indian Army's first heliborne operation, near Sylhet.

cites.loc: para 5
"He witnessed in Dhaka the signing of the surrender instrument"

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: Present at the surrender
claims.text: He was present in Dhaka when General Niazi signed the instrument of surrender on 16 December 1971.

claims.heading: "Jaggi, over my dead body"
claims.text: He is said to have answered Lt Gen J S Aurora's order to halt at the Meghna with "Jaggi, over my dead body", in a telephone conversation.
claims.unresolved: Still unverified. The SSRF founder reports that the exchange took place by telephone but that the exact words are not confirmed, and it has not been found in A Talent for War so far. Do not quote the words as his until a source is found.

cites.loc: 1972 table: "Sagat Singh"
the two civil-list notifications of January 1972 do not include him; the war awards were notified separately
"to be so awarded in 1971" (incorrect year)
gives 1976 (incorrect year)
para 5

claims.established: He received the Padma Bhushan in 1972, for the 1971 war.
claims.heading: The year of the Padma Bhushan

prev.text: He received the Padma Bhushan for the 1971 campaign.

claims.text: He received the Padma Bhushan in 1972 for the 1971 campaign.
claims.unresolved: Settled on 1972. The SSRF founder confirms 1972 from the government's official list of recipients; the year-wise list agrees. The 1971 (Wikipedia biography) and 1976 (Live History India) dates are wrong. Still wanted: the Gazette notification number for the 1971-war awards, which the online 1972 file does not contain.

claims.established: IV Corps crossed the Meghna by helicopter on its advance to Dhaka.
claims.heading: The order to halt at the Meghna
claims.text: IV Corps's formal orders were to halt at the Meghna and secure the territory on its near bank. Sagat Singh went beyond them and crossed the river by helicopter.
claims.unresolved: The SSRF founder's account (15 November 2026). Needs a citable source for the halt order: a page in A Talent for War, Eastern Command or IV Corps orders, or a published account by an officer involved.

cites.loc: "in July 1965 … general officer commanding"
"In December 1967, Singh was appointed GOC 101 Communication Zone"
names him GOC 17th Mountain Division in 1967

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: Command of 17 Mountain Division
claims.text: He commanded 17 Mountain Division in Sikkim from July 1965 to December 1967.

cites.loc: p. 74: refused to vacate Nathu La when the corps ordered the passes vacated in 1965; Jelep La was vacated
"Major General Sagat Singh, GOC 17 Mountain Division, refused to vacate Nathu La"

claims.established: In 1965 he refused a corps instruction to vacate Nathu La; Jelep La, which was vacated, has been under Chinese control since (A Talent for War, p. 74).
claims.heading: Refusal to vacate Nathu La
claims.text: In 1965 the corps headquarters instructed that the Sikkim passes be vacated. Sagat Singh refused to vacate Nathu La. Jelep La was vacated, and it has remained under Chinese control since.
claims.unresolved: Settled: the biography (p. 74) and the UNI report agree that the instruction came from corps headquarters in 1965. Still to record: the exact date of the instruction.

cites.loc: "the Nathu La and Cho La clashes took place, where 17 Mountain Division achieved"
59th Nathula Vijay Diwas, 11 September 2025

claims.established: As stated.
claims.heading: The 1967 clashes
claims.text: His division held Nathu La and Cho La in the clashes with Chinese troops in 1967. Sikkim marks 11 September as Nathula Vijay Diwas.

campaigns.background: Portugal kept Goa, Daman and Diu after Indian independence and refused to negotiate their transfer. In December 1961 India ordered military action, named Operation Vijay.

chronology.e: Promoted brigadier; takes command of 50 (Independent) Parachute Brigade
2 Sikh LI enters Panjim; 1 Para reaches the Governor's house

campaigns.commandNote: Whether 50 Parachute Brigade came under 17 Infantry Division or directly under Southern Command is to be confirmed. Grey entries are not yet checked against a source.
disagreements: Whether the brigade's task was a supporting advance from the north or the capture of Panaji.
campaigns.lead: In December 1961 his 50 (Independent) Parachute Brigade advanced into Goa and reached Panjim on 19 December, the day Portuguese rule ended.
campaigns.mapWanted: Historical maps of Operation Vijay, or the brigade's own route sketches, are wanted.
campaigns.name: Liberation of Goa, 1961
campaigns.objectives: Not yet researched. The brigade's assigned objective is itself an open question (see below).
campaigns.role: He had taken over the brigade three months earlier, an infantry officer from the 3rd Gorkha Rifles, and led it in Operation Vijay.
campaigns.significance: SSRF assessment: Goa made his name for speed and initiative, a pattern repeated at Nathu La and on the Meghna. The state he helped liberate has no public memorial to him.
unknowns: Which battalions of 50 Parachute Brigade took which routes, and on what timings.
The brigade's written orders and war diary for 17 to 19 December 1961.
Whether a Portuguese record of a bounty exists.
Why Goa has no public memorial to him.

milestones.label: 2 Sikh Light Infantry, under his command, was first into Panjim; 1 Para was first to the Governor's house.
The bounty Salazar's government put on his head for his part in the liberation of Goa.
How long he had commanded 50 (Independent) Parachute Brigade before Operation Vijay.

campaigns.background: The war on India's eastern front began on 3 December 1971. The Meghna, one of the widest rivers in the delta, lay between IV Corps and Dhaka.

chronology.e: Takes command of IV Corps at Tezpur
War begins on the eastern front
Pakistani surrender in Dhaka, which he witnesses

command.name: Army Headquarters
command.who: Gen Sam Manekshaw, Chief of the Army Staff

command.name: 8 Mountain Division
command.who: Maj Gen K V Krishna Rao

campaigns.commandNote: Live History India names Maj Gen B F Gonsalves but not his division; his command of 57 Mountain Division is yet to be checked.

decisions.c: Opened the road to Dhaka from the east.
decisions.d: Airlift troops across the Meghna instead of waiting for the bridge to be repaired
Land troops by helicopter near Sylhet

disagreements: Whether the formal orders were to halt at the Meghna, and the "Jaggi, over my dead body" exchange, said to have been by telephone, exact words unconfirmed.
campaigns.lead: Given IV Corps in December 1970, he took it across the Meghna by helicopter in December 1971 and was in Dhaka for the Pakistani surrender.
campaigns.mapWanted: Original operational maps of the Meghna crossing are wanted.
campaigns.name: The Meghna crossing and the road to Dhaka, 1971
campaigns.objectives: Not yet researched. Whether Dhaka was an early objective of IV Corps is itself debated.
campaigns.role: He commanded IV Corps throughout, conceived the Army's first heliborne operation near Sylhet, and with Maj Gen B F Gonsalves decided to airlift troops across the Meghna.
campaigns.significance: SSRF assessment: the helicopter lifts let IV Corps cross river lines that were expected to hold it, and brought Indian troops to the approaches of Dhaka before the surrender on 16 December 1971.
unknowns: How many sorties the helicopters flew across the Meghna, and over how many nights.
The written orders between IV Corps and Eastern Command from 8 to 12 December 1971.
Which units were lifted, and to which landing areas.

milestones.label: The Indian Army's first heliborne operation, near Sylhet, which he conceived.
With the bridge out of use, troops were lifted across the river by helicopter instead of waiting for repairs.
The Pakistani surrender in Dhaka, which he witnessed.

campaigns.background: Five years after the 1962 war, Indian and Chinese troops faced each other along the Sikkim–Tibet border, where the passes of Nathu La and Cho La lie on the watershed.

chronology.e: Promoted major general; takes command of 17 Mountain Division
Clash at Nathu La; the date is now observed as Nathula Vijay Diwas

campaigns.commandNote: As in 1967, from Fair Observer (2019). Brigades and battalions are yet to be documented.

decisions.c: The pass stayed in Indian hands and was held in 1967.

disagreements: Whether he was promoted in 1964 or 1965.
campaigns.lead: As GOC 17 Mountain Division he refused to give up Nathu La, and in 1967 his division held it and Cho La when Chinese troops attacked.
campaigns.mapWanted: A map of the Sikkim passes with the 1967 positions is wanted.
campaigns.name: Nathu La and Cho La, 1965 to 1967
campaigns.role: He commanded the division responsible for the Sikkim passes from July 1965 to December 1967.
campaigns.significance: SSRF assessment: the clashes showed that Indian troops could hold their ground against the Chinese army five years after 1962. Sikkim observes Nathula Vijay Diwas every 11 September.
unknowns: The battalions engaged at Nathu La and Cho La, and their casualties.
The division's war diary for September and October 1967.
The exact date in 1965 of the corps instruction to vacate the passes.

milestones.label: He refused the order to vacate Nathu La. Jelep La, which was vacated, has been under Chinese control since.
Clash at Nathu La. Sikkim observes the date as Nathula Vijay Diwas.
Clash at Cho La. His division held both passes.
